l: first covenant, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 8
s: The first covenant is the one the Lord made with the fathers of Israel when he took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt; they did not continue in it. It is said not to have been faultless, since a second was sought, and the announcement of a new covenant has made it obsolete, aged, and near to vanishing away.

l: new covenant, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 8
s: The new covenant is the better covenant of which the high priest is mediator, given on better promises. The Lord promises to make it with the house of Israel and the house of Judah after those days, putting his laws in their minds and hearts, so that all will know him from least to greatest, and showing mercy by remembering their sins no more.

l: house of Israel, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 8
s: The house of Israel, together with the house of Judah, is the party with whom the Lord promises to make a new covenant. They will have his laws put into their minds and written on their hearts, will be his people, and will all know him from least to greatest.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 9
s: Chapter 9 compares the first covenant's earthly worship with Christ's work. The first covenant had an earthly sanctuary whose tabernacle was divided into the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies, where priests served continually and the high priest entered alone once a year with blood for himself and the people's errors. Christ, as high priest of the coming good things, entered the greater and more perfect tabernacle once for all through his own blood, obtaining eternal redemption and cleansing the conscience. Because a death occurred for the transgressions under the first covenant, he is mediator of a new covenant, just as the first covenant was dedicated with blood by Moses and nearly everything is cleansed with blood. Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many and will appear a second time to save those who eagerly wait for him.

l: Christ, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 9
s: Christ came as high priest of the coming good things and entered the heavenly Holy Place once for all through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption. He offered himself without defect to God through the eternal Spirit, was revealed once at the end of the ages to put away sin, and will appear a second time to save those eagerly waiting for him.

l: first covenant, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 9
s: The first covenant had ordinances of divine service and an earthly sanctuary, with fleshly ordinances imposed until a time of reformation. It was dedicated with blood when Moses sprinkled the book and the people, saying 'This is the blood of the covenant which God has commanded you.' Its gifts and sacrifices could not make the worshiper perfect in conscience.

l: new covenant, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 9
s: Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, since a death occurred for the redemption of transgressions under the first covenant. Through it those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. The text compares it to a will, which is in force only after the death of the one who made it.

l: earthly tabernacle (the tabernacle Moses made), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 9
s: The earthly tabernacle was prepared with a first part, the Holy Place, holding the lamp stand, table and show bread, and behind the second veil the Holy of Holies, holding the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant. Priests went continually into the first, while the high priest alone entered the second once a year. Its standing signified that the way into the Holy Place was not yet revealed, and it and its vessels were sprinkled with blood.

l: greater and more perfect tabernacle (heavenly), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 9
s: The greater and more perfect tabernacle is not made with hands and not of this creation. Christ passed through it into heaven itself, the true holy place, to appear in God's presence for us. The earthly holy places are representations or copies of it.

l: high priest (Levitical), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 9
s: The Levitical high priest alone entered the second tabernacle, once in the year, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the errors of the people. He enters the holy place year by year with blood not his own. His repeated entry contrasts with Christ's single offering of himself.

l: blood, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 9
s: Blood is central to cleansing and covenant: the first covenant was dedicated with the blood of calves and goats, and apart from shedding of blood there is no remission. The blood of goats and bulls sanctifies to the cleanness of the flesh, but the blood of Christ cleanses the conscience from dead works to serve the living God. Christ entered the Holy Place through his own blood, not that of goats and calves.

l: sacrifices, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 9
s: The gifts and sacrifices of the first covenant were incapable of making the worshiper perfect concerning the conscience. The copies of heavenly things were cleansed with such sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves required better sacrifices. Christ's single sacrifice of himself puts away sin and need not be repeated, unlike the yearly offerings.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 10
s: Chapter 10 argues that the law, a mere shadow of good things to come, could never perfect worshipers through its repeated yearly sacrifices, since the blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins. Jesus Christ, quoted as coming to do God's will with a prepared body, takes away the first order and establishes the second by offering his body once for all, then sits at God's right hand awaiting his enemies' subjection. The Holy Spirit testifies to the new covenant, in which God writes his laws on hearts and remembers sins no more, so no further offering for sin remains. The writer urges the brothers to draw near with faith through the blood of Jesus, hold fast their hope, and encourage one another, warns of fearful judgment for willful sin and for trampling the Son of God, and calls the readers to recall their past endurance and not shrink back but live by faith.

l: Christ, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 10
s: Jesus Christ comes into the world with a body prepared for him to do God's will, and through the offering of that body once for all he sanctifies believers. Having offered one sacrifice for sins forever, he sat down at God's right hand, waiting until his enemies become his footstool. By his blood and through the veil of his flesh he opened a new and living way into the holy place, and he is the great priest over God's house.

l: God, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 10
s: God is shown as having no pleasure in sacrifices and burnt offerings under the law, but preparing a body for the one who comes to do his will. He promises through the new covenant to put his laws on hearts and minds and to remember sins no more. He is faithful to his promise, claims vengeance and judgment of his people, and is called the living God, into whose hands it is fearful to fall.

l: law (Moses' law), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 10
s: The law is described as a shadow of the good to come, not the very image of the things, and it cannot perfect those who draw near. Its sacrifices are taken away as the first order so that the second may be established. A person who disregards Moses' law dies without compassion on the word of two or three witnesses.

l: sacrifices (offered under the law), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 10
s: The sacrifices are offered year by year and day by day by priests who stand serving, repeating the same offerings. They can never take away sins, because the blood of bulls and goats cannot do so, and they serve only as a yearly reminder of sins. God did not desire them, and Christ's one sacrifice replaces them.

l: new covenant, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 10
s: The new covenant is quoted from the Lord through the testimony of the Holy Spirit: after those days God will put his laws on their heart and write them on their mind. Under it God will remember their sins and iniquities no more. Because remission is given, there is no more offering for sin.

l: sins, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 10
s: Sins are not taken away by the blood of bulls and goats, and the law's sacrifices only remind of them each year. Christ's one offering deals with them for good, and God promises to remember them no more, so no further offering for sin is needed. Willfully sinning after receiving knowledge of the truth leaves no sacrifice for sins.

l: readers (addressees of the letter), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 10
s: The readers, addressed as brothers, are urged to enter the holy place by Jesus' blood, draw near with a true heart in full faith, hold fast their confession, and provoke one another to love and good works without forsaking assembling together. They are reminded of their earlier endurance after being enlightened: reproaches, oppressions, compassion for the writer in chains, and joyful acceptance of plundered possessions. They are told not to throw away their boldness, to endure to receive the promise, and are counted among those who have faith to the saving of the soul rather than those who shrink back.

l: faith, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 10
s: Faith is the basis for drawing near to God in fullness, and the righteous one will live by faith. God has no pleasure in one who shrinks back. The writer says his group is not of those who shrink back to destruction but of those who have faith to the saving of the soul.

l: willful sin and judgment, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 10
s: If people sin willfully after receiving knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains, only a fearful expectation of judgment and a fierceness of fire that will devour the adversaries. Whoever tramples the Son of God, counts the covenant blood an unholy thing, and insults the Spirit of grace deserves much worse punishment than one who disregarded Moses' law. The Lord says vengeance is his and he will judge his people, and it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 11
s: Chapter 11 defines faith as assurance of things hoped for and proof of things not seen, and says the elders obtained approval by it. It surveys people who acted by faith: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, the Israelites who crossed the Red Sea and circled Jericho, and Rahab. Abraham is given the most attention: he obeyed the call without knowing where he went, lived as an alien in tents, looked for a city built by God, and offered up Isaac believing God could raise the dead. Moses refused to be called Pharaoh's daughter's son, left Egypt, and kept the Passover. The chapter closes with unnamed believers who conquered or suffered, and says none of them received the promise, since God provided something better so that they would be made perfect together with us.

l: God, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 11
s: God is the one by whose word the universe was framed, and he is well pleased by faith, since those who come to him must believe he exists and rewards those who seek him. He gave testimony to Abel's gifts, translated Enoch, and promised Abraham, Sarah and their heirs. He is not ashamed to be called the God of those seeking a heavenly country, has prepared a city for them, and has provided something better concerning 'us' so that the earlier believers are not made perfect apart from us.

l: faith, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 11
s: Faith is defined as assurance of things hoped for and proof of things not seen, and through it the elders obtained approval. Without it, it is impossible to be well pleasing to God. It is shown in a long series of examples, from Abel and Noah to Abraham, Moses, and Rahab, and in those who subdued kingdoms or endured torture, though none of them received the promise.

l: Abraham, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 11
s: Abraham obeyed when called and went out to an inheritance without knowing where he was going. He lived as an alien in the land of promise, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, and looked for the city whose builder and maker is God. Tested, he offered up Isaac, his only born son, concluding that God is able to raise the dead; one man, as good as dead, fathered descendants as numerous as the stars and sand.

l: Moses, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 11
s: Moses was hidden for three months by his parents, who saw he was a beautiful child and did not fear the king's commandment. When grown, he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, chose ill treatment with God's people over the pleasures of sin, and counted the reproach of Christ greater riches than Egypt's treasures. By faith he left Egypt without fearing the king's wrath and kept the Passover and the sprinkling of the blood.

l: elders, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 11
s: The elders obtained approval by faith. The chapter's list of examples illustrates what that approval rested on, and it says these all, commended for their faith, did not receive the promise.

l: heavenly country, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 11
s: The heavenly country is the better country that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and others desired, as strangers and pilgrims on the earth, rather than the country they had left. Because they seek it, God is not ashamed to be called their God, and he has prepared a city for them.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 12
s: Chapter 12 urges its readers, surrounded by a cloud of witnesses, to lay aside every weight and sin and run with perseverance while looking to Jesus, who endured the cross and sat down at the right hand of God's throne. It reframes the readers' hardships as the discipline of a loving Father, which is painful for the present but yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness and shares God's holiness. The readers are told to lift their hands and knees, make straight paths, pursue peace and sanctification, and guard against falling short of God's grace, as Esau did when he sold his birthright and found no place for a change of mind. The chapter contrasts the terrifying mountain that burned with fire, where Moses was terrified, with Mount Zion, the city of the living God, where Jesus mediates a new covenant and his blood of sprinkling speaks better than Abel's. It closes by warning the readers not to refuse the God who speaks from heaven, who promises to shake earth and heavens once more, and urges them to serve God with reverence and awe because they receive a Kingdom that can't be shaken and because God is a consuming fire.

l: Christ, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 12
s: Jesus is called the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despised its shame, and sat down at the right hand of God's throne. He is also named the mediator of a new covenant, whose blood of sprinkling speaks better than that of Abel. The readers are told to look to him and consider how he endured such contradiction from sinners so they won't grow weary.

l: God, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 12
s: God is presented as a Father who disciplines those he loves and receives as sons, for their profit, so that they may share his holiness. He is called the Father of spirits, the Judge of all, and the living God whose city is the heavenly Jerusalem. He spoke on earth and now warns from heaven, has promised to shake not only the earth but also the heavens, and is described as a consuming fire.

l: Mount Zion, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 12
s: Mount Zion is where the readers have come, together with the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. It is associated with innumerable angels, the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, God the Judge, the spirits of just men made perfect, and Jesus the mediator of a new covenant.

l: mountain (Sinai, that burned with fire), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 12
s: This mountain is described as one that might be touched and that burned with fire, with blackness, darkness, storm, a trumpet sound, and a voice of words. Those who heard begged for no more words, since they could not stand the command that even an animal touching it be stoned. The appearance was so fearful that Moses said he was terrified and trembling. The readers are told they have not come to this mountain.

l: readers (the audience addressed), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 12
s: The readers are exhorted to run the race with perseverance, endure discipline as God's children, lift their drooping hands and feeble knees, and pursue peace and sanctification. They are warned against falling short of God's grace, bitterness, sexual immorality, and profanity like Esau's, and against refusing the one who speaks. They are told they have come to Mount Zion rather than the burning mountain, and are to serve God acceptably with reverence and awe, since they receive an unshakable Kingdom.

l: discipline, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 12
s: Discipline is explained as the sign that God treats the readers as true sons, since a son without discipline is illegitimate. Earthly fathers disciplined for a few days as seemed good to them, but God does so for the readers' profit, that they may share his holiness. Though grievous for the present, it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it.

l: Kingdom that can't be shaken, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 12
s: The readers are said to be receiving a Kingdom that can't be shaken. This is set against God's promise to shake earth and heavens once more, which signifies the removal of made things so that what is not shaken may remain. In response, the readers are to have grace and serve God acceptably with reverence and awe.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 13
s: Chapter 13 closes the letter with practical exhortations to its readers: continue brotherly love, show hospitality to strangers, remember prisoners and the ill-treated, honor marriage, and be free from the love of money, trusting God's promise never to forsake them. Readers are told to remember and imitate their leaders' faith, to obey them, and to avoid strange teachings about foods, since Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. The text says Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people with his blood, so the readers are urged to go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach, and to offer a sacrifice of praise and of doing good and sharing. The author asks for prayer, hopes to be restored to the readers soon, and mentions that Timothy has been freed. The chapter ends with a blessing from the God of peace, greetings from the Italians, and a prayer for grace.

l: Christ, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 13
s: Jesus Christ is described as the same yesterday, today, and forever. He suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood, and God brought him again from the dead as the great shepherd of the sheep with the blood of an eternal covenant.

l: God, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 13
s: God is said to have promised never to leave or forsake the readers, and he is well pleased with the sacrifices of doing good and sharing. He is called the God of peace, who brought Jesus back from the dead, and the author prays he will make the readers complete in every good work and work in them what pleases him, with glory to him forever.

l: leaders, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 13
s: The leaders spoke the word of God to the readers, and the readers are told to remember them, imitate their faith, obey them, and submit to them. They watch on behalf of the readers' souls and will give account, so the readers are urged to make their work a joy rather than a groaning. The readers are also told to greet them.

l: readers (the addressees), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 13
s: The readers are given instructions to love one another, show hospitality, remember prisoners, honor marriage, be content, and not be carried away by strange teachings about foods. They are urged to go out to Jesus outside the camp, offer a sacrifice of praise, do good and share, obey their leaders, and pray for the author, and they receive greetings from the Italians and a closing blessing.

l: outside the camp, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 13
s: Outside the camp is where the bodies of the animals whose blood the high priest brings into the holy place are burned. Jesus suffered outside the gate, and the readers are urged to go out to him there, bearing his reproach, since they have no enduring city here.

l: sacrifice of praise, The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 13
s: The readers are told to offer a sacrifice of praise to God continually through Jesus. It is defined as the fruit of lips that proclaim allegiance to his name, and it is joined with doing good and sharing as sacrifices that please God.

l: author (writer of the letter), The Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 13
s: The author asks the readers to pray for him and those with him, claiming a good conscience and a desire to live honorably. He hopes to be restored to them soon, says he has written in few words and exhorts them to endure the word of exhortation, and reports that Timothy has been freed and may come with him to see them.

l: Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter / Chapter 1
s: Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, writes to those who share a precious faith with him, wishing them grace and peace through knowledge of God and Jesus. He explains that God's divine power has granted all things pertaining to life and godliness and given great promises so believers may partake of the divine nature. He urges his readers to add to their faith a series of virtues, ending in love, warning that lacking them means blindness while having them secures their calling and entrance into the eternal Kingdom. Peter says he will keep reminding them because his departure is coming soon, as Jesus made clear to him. He grounds his message in eyewitness testimony of Christ's majesty, including the voice from heaven on the holy mountain, and affirms that Scripture's prophecy came from men moved by the Holy Spirit, not private interpretation.

l: Simon Peter, Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter / Chapter 1
s: Simon Peter identifies himself as a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ writing to fellow believers. He urges diligence, promises to keep reminding them of these things as long as he is in his tent, and will strive so they can remember after his departure. He claims to be an eyewitness of Christ's majesty who heard the voice from heaven on the holy mountain.

l: Jesus Christ, Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter / Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is called Lord and Savior, and knowledge of him is where grace and peace are multiplied and where believers are made fruitful. He made clear to Peter that Peter's departure would come swiftly. He received honor and glory from God the Father, and the apostles were eyewitnesses of his majesty. His eternal Kingdom is the place believers are richly supplied entrance to.

l: God, Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter / Chapter 1
s: God, through his divine power, has granted all things pertaining to life and godliness and called believers by his own glory and virtue. He has given precious and exceedingly great promises so that believers may partake of the divine nature. As the Father, he gave Jesus honor and glory, and the Majestic Glory voice declared Jesus his beloved Son in whom he is well pleased.

l: recipients of the letter (Peter's readers), Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter / Chapter 1
s: Peter's readers are those who have obtained a like precious faith with the apostles. They are told to add diligently to their faith, to make their calling and election sure so they will never stumble, and to heed the prophetic word. Peter says they already know these things and are established in the present truth.

l: virtues to add to faith, Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter / Chapter 1
s: Peter lists a progression: in faith supply moral excellence, then knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love. If these abound, they keep believers from being idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of Jesus Christ. Whoever lacks them is blind, seeing only what is near and forgetting cleansing from old sins.

l: Peter's death (departure), Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter / Chapter 1
s: Peter describes his death as the putting off of his tent, which comes swiftly, as Jesus Christ made clear to him. It motivates him to stir up his readers by reminding them now. He will make every effort so they can remember these things after his departure.

l: transfiguration voice experience, Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter / Chapter 1
s: Peter recounts that the apostles heard a voice come from the Majestic Glory out of heaven when they were with Jesus on the holy mountain. The voice said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Peter cites it as eyewitness proof that their message was not cunningly devised fables.

l: prophecy of Scripture, Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter / Chapter 1
s: Prophecy is called the more sure word, which readers do well to heed as a lamp shining in a dark place until the day dawns and the morning star arises in their hearts. Peter states that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation. It never came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke, moved by the Holy Spirit.

l: Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 warns that false teachers, like the false prophets of old, will secretly bring destructive heresies among the readers, deny the Master, and exploit people through greed and deceptive words. It cites God's past judgments as proof that punishment is certain: the angels who sinned were cast into Tartarus, the ancient world was flooded while Noah and seven others were preserved, and Sodom and Gomorrah were turned to ashes while righteous Lot was delivered. The text concludes that the Lord knows how to deliver the godly and keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment. The false teachers are described as lustful, arrogant, and despising authority, following the way of Balaam, and likened to waterless wells and storm-driven clouds. They promise liberty while being slaves of corruption, and those who knew the way of righteousness and turned back are compared to a dog returning to its vomit and a washed sow wallowing in the mire.

l: false teachers, Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 2
s: False teachers will secretly bring in destructive heresies, deny the Master who bought them, and exploit people in covetousness with deceptive words, leading many to follow their immoral ways. They are described as daring, self-willed, despising authority, reveling in deceit, and following the way of Balaam, and they promise liberty while being bondservants of corruption. Their destruction is certain, and the blackness of darkness is reserved for them, with their last state worse than the first, like a dog returning to its vomit.

l: God, Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 2
s: God did not spare the angels who sinned, casting them down to Tartarus and committing them to pits of darkness for judgment. He also did not spare the ancient world, preserving Noah with seven others, and condemned Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes while delivering righteous Lot. The text states that the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation and keep the unrighteous under punishment.

l: day of the Lord (judgment), Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 2
s: The day of judgment is the time for which the unrighteous are kept under punishment, as the Lord knows how to do. The sinning angels are likewise reserved in pits of darkness for judgment, and the text presents past judgments as examples that the false teachers' destruction will not slumber.

l: Peter’s Second Letter, Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 3
s: The writer addresses his beloved readers in a second letter, reminding them of the words of the holy prophets and the apostles' commandment. He warns that in the last days mockers will walk after their own lusts and ask where the promise of Christ's coming is, willfully forgetting that God's word created the earth and flooded the world. The same word has reserved the present heavens and earth for fire on the day of judgment. The writer explains that the Lord is patient, not wishing anyone to perish but all to come to repentance, though the day of the Lord will come as a thief. He urges holy living, diligence to be found in peace, and watchfulness against error, and he closes by calling the readers to grow in the grace and knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, to whom be glory.

l: Jesus Christ, Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 3
s: He is the one whose coming is promised and mocked, and the apostles are described as his apostles. The readers are told to grow in his grace and knowledge, and glory is ascribed to him both now and forever.

l: God, Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 3
s: By his word the heavens and the earth were formed out of water and amid water, and by the same word the world of that time was destroyed by flood. By that word the present heavens and earth are stored up for fire, reserved for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men.

l: recipients of the letter (Peter's readers), Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 3
s: They receive a second letter meant to stir up their sincere minds, and they are told to remember the prophets' words and the apostles' commandment. They are urged to live in holiness and godliness, to be diligent to be found in peace, without defect and blameless, to beware of being carried away by the error of the wicked, and to grow in grace and knowledge.

l: mockers (last days), Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 3
s: They will come in the last days, walking after their own lusts, and will ask where the promise of his coming is, claiming all things continue as from the beginning of creation. The text says they willfully forget that God's word made the heavens and earth and brought the flood.

l: day of the Lord (judgment), Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 3
s: It will come as a thief in the night, when the heavens pass away with a great noise, the elements dissolve with fervent heat, and the earth and its works are burned up. It is the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men, and it is called the day of God, which believers look for and earnestly desire.

l: promise of his coming, Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 3
s: Mockers question it, pointing to the fact that all things have continued unchanged since the fathers fell asleep. The writer answers that the Lord is not slow but patient, wishing all to come to repentance, and that a day with the Lord is as a thousand years.

l: new heavens and a new earth, Peter’s Second Letter, Chapter 3
s: According to his promise, believers look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells. This hope is the basis for the exhortation to be diligent to be found in peace, without defect and blameless.

l: Jude, Jude, Jude / Chapter 1
s: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes to those who are called, urging them to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints. He warns that certain ungodly men have crept in secretly, turning God's grace into indecency and denying Jesus Christ. Jude cites examples of judgment: the people saved out of Egypt who didn't believe, angels who deserted their dwelling, Sodom and Gomorrah, and Cain, Balaam, and Korah, and he quotes Enoch's prophecy of the Lord's coming to judge the ungodly. He calls the intruders murmurers, mockers, and causers of divisions, as the apostles foretold. He then exhorts the beloved to build themselves up in faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, show varied compassion to others, and closes with praise to God who is able to keep them from stumbling.

l: Jude, Jude, Jude / Chapter 1
s: Jude identifies himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, and writes to those who are called. Though eager to write about common salvation, he felt constrained to exhort them to contend for the faith, warn them about intruders, and urge them to build themselves up, closing with a doxology to God.

l: Jesus Christ, Jude, Jude / Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is the one Jude serves, and those called are kept for him. The intruders deny him as the only Master and Lord, the apostles spoke of him beforehand, and believers are to look for his mercy leading to eternal life.

l: God, Jude, Jude / Chapter 1
s: God the Father sanctifies those who are called, and he is described as our Savior who alone is wise, to whom glory, majesty, dominion and power belong. The text says the Lord saved a people out of Egypt and afterward destroyed unbelievers, keeps deserting angels in everlasting bonds, and will come to execute judgment on all the ungodly; he is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them faultless in great joy.

l: recipients (those called, beloved), Jude, Jude / Chapter 1
s: The recipients are called, sanctified by God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ, and Jude wishes them mercy, peace, and love multiplied. They are told to remember the apostles' words, build themselves up on their most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, and show compassion to some while saving others from the fire with fear.

l: intruders (certain ungodly men), Jude, Jude / Chapter 1
s: These men crept in secretly, were long ago written about for condemnation, turn God's grace into indecency, and deny Jesus Christ. They defile the flesh, despise authority, slander celestial beings, speak evil of what they don't know, follow the ways of Cain, Balaam, and Korah, and are compared to hidden reefs, waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves, and wandering stars. They are murmurers, mockers, and divisive, sensual people without the Spirit, and blackness of darkness is reserved for them.

l: faith, Jude, Jude / Chapter 1
s: The faith is described as the one once for all delivered to the saints, and Jude urges the recipients to contend earnestly for it. It is also called their most holy faith, on which they are to keep building themselves up.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew
s: This is the Gospel According to Matthew, chapters 1 to 28, a narrative of the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. It opens with his genealogy from Abraham and David through Joseph, and his birth to Mary by the Holy Spirit. Wise men seek him, Herod massacres the children of Bethlehem, and the family flees to Egypt before settling in Nazareth. John the Baptizer preaches repentance and baptizes Jesus, and God's voice names him beloved Son. After forty days of fasting and three temptations answered with Scripture, Jesus begins preaching in Galilee and calls Peter, Andrew, James, and John. Chapters 5 to 7 give his long teaching on the mountain: the Beatitudes, fulfilling the law, love of enemies, secret piety, the model prayer, freedom from anxiety, and obedience, ending with the houses on rock and sand. Chapters 8 to 10 show healings, calming the storm, calling Matthew, and the sending of the twelve apostles with warnings of persecution. Chapters 11 to 14 present John's question from prison, growing opposition from the Pharisees, parables of the Kingdom, John's beheading under Herod, the feeding of five thousand, and Jesus walking on the sea. Chapters 15 to 17 include disputes over tradition, the Canaanite woman, the feeding of four thousand, Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ, the first predictions of suffering, and the transfiguration. Chapters 18 to 20 teach humility, forgiveness, marriage, riches, and serving, through parables such as the unforgiving servant and the vineyard laborers, while Jesus again predicts his death. In chapters 21 to 23 he enters Jerusalem to cries of 'Hosanna', cleanses the temple, is challenged by priests, Pharisees, Sadducees, and Herodians, names the greatest commandment, and pronounces woes on the scribes and Pharisees. Chapters 24 and 25 are his teaching on the end of the age: signs, watchfulness, and the parables of the ten virgins, the talents, and the sheep and goats. Chapters 26 and 27 narrate the Passover meal, Judas's betrayal, Gethsemane, arrest, trial before Caiaphas, Peter's denial, Pilate's judgment, the choice of Barabbas, crucifixion at Golgotha, his death with signs of darkness and an earthquake, and burial in Joseph of Arimathaea's tomb, which is guarded and sealed. Chapter 28 closes with the empty tomb, the angel's announcement to Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, the priests' bribe to the guards, and Jesus's commission to the eleven on a Galilean mountain to make disciples of all nations, with the promise to be with them always.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Jesus is the central figure of these records, presented as Jesus Christ: son of David and Abraham, firstborn of Mary, conceived by the Holy Spirit, named by Joseph at the angel's command, and called Immanuel, 'God with us', who will save his people from their sins. He is born in Bethlehem in the days of King Herod, called King of the Jews by the wise men, taken to Egypt, and raised in Nazareth, so that he is called a Nazarene. He comes from Galilee to be baptized by John, who is less mighty than he; the Spirit of God descends and a voice calls him beloved Son. He fasts forty days and nights, resists temptation, then settles in Capernaum, preaches repentance and the Kingdom of Heaven, teaches in synagogues, and calls Simon Peter, Andrew, James and John. His ministry shows authority: he teaches as one with authority, casts out demons, calms the storm, heals many, and forgives sins as the Son of Man. He feels compassion for the multitudes, appoints twelve disciples and sends them to the lost sheep of Israel. He is accused of gluttony and called friend of tax collectors and sinners, yet describes himself as gentle and humble in heart, giving rest to the weary. He claims a unique relationship with the Father, who has delivered all things to him. He is Lord of the Sabbath and greater than the temple, Jonah and Solomon, though rejected in his own country, where his mother, brothers and carpenter father are named. Peter confesses him as the Christ; he is transfigured, his face shining like the sun, and the voice again names him beloved Son. He foretells his death and resurrection, leaves Galilee, goes up to Jerusalem, and enters as a humble King on a donkey, acclaimed Son of David. He debates opponents, teaches on the Mount of Olives, keeps Passover with his disciples, and before the high priest affirms he is the Christ, the Son of God. He is accused as King of the Jews, crucified, and buried by Joseph of Arimathaea. The angel announces him risen. In Galilee he tells the eleven that all authority in heaven and on earth is given to him, commands them to make disciples, and promises to be with them to the end of the age.

l: Abraham, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: father_of Isaac Abraham stands at the head of the genealogy, becoming the father of Isaac. Jesus Christ is called his son, and the generations from Abraham to David are counted as fourteen.

l: David, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: David is a king, son of Jesse, who fathered Solomon by Uriah's wife and ate show bread unlawfully. Matthew places him in Jesus's lineage: Jesus Christ and Joseph are called his sons, with fourteen generations to the exile. Jesus quotes David, speaking in the Spirit, calling the Christ Lord.

l: Joseph, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Joseph is a righteous man, son of Jacob and husband of Mary, whose son Jesus is born. Initially planning to quietly put Mary away when she is found pregnant, he follows an angel's dream message, takes her as wife, and names the child Jesus. Warned in dreams, he protects the family by taking them to Egypt by night, later returns after Herod's death, and, fearing Archelaus, withdraws to Galilee and settles in Nazareth.

l: Mary, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Mary is the mother of Jesus Christ. Engaged to Joseph, she is found pregnant by the Holy Spirit before they come together; Joseph takes her as wife and she bears her firstborn son. Wise men see her with the child, then Joseph takes her to Egypt, back to Israel, and to Nazareth.

l: Holy Spirit, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The Holy Spirit is the divine agent in Matthew: first the source of Mary's conception, as the angel tells Joseph, then, after Jesus's baptism, seen as the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming on him.

l: angel of the Lord, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: appears_to Joseph [in a dream] An angel of the Lord appears to Joseph in a dream, telling him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife because her child is conceived of the Holy Spirit. He instructs Joseph to name the son Jesus, and Joseph does as the angel commanded.

l: genealogy of Jesus Christ, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The genealogy of Jesus Christ in Matthew 1 traces descent from Abraham through David, Solomon, and Judah's kings to the Babylonian exile, then Shealtiel, Zerubbabel, Jacob, and Joseph, Mary's husband. It is organized as three sets of fourteen generations, ending at the Christ.

l: birth of Jesus Christ, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The birth of Jesus Christ is described as occurring after Mary's engagement to Joseph, when she is found pregnant by the Holy Spirit. It is said to fulfill the Lord's word through the prophet about a virgin bearing a son called Immanuel, and Joseph names the child Jesus after he is born.

l: Herod, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Herod is a king troubled by news of a newborn King of the Jews. He consults priests and scribes, deceives the wise men, then, mocked by their departure, orders Bethlehem's boys aged two and under killed. He later dies, and his son Archelaus reigns in Judea.

l: wise men, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Wise men from the east travel to Jerusalem seeking the newborn King of the Jews after seeing his star; they find the child, worship him with gold, frankincense and myrrh, then, warned in a dream, avoid Herod and return home another way.

l: Bethlehem, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Bethlehem, a town in Judea, is the prophesied birthplace of the Christ; Jesus is born there, Herod sends the wise men to it, and he later has its male children killed.

l: Jerusalem, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Jerusalem is the city Jesus enters in Chapter 21, where the whole city is stirred and asks who he is, and crowds name him the prophet from Nazareth. In Chapter 23 he rebukes it as the killer of prophets and stoner of those sent to her, laments her unwilling children, and leaves her house desolate until she blesses him.

l: Egypt, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Egypt is where Joseph takes the child and Mary by night to escape Herod's plan to destroy him. They stay there until Herod's death, fulfilling the words "Out of Egypt I called my son," and an angel appears to Joseph there to tell him to return.

l: Nazareth, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Nazareth is a city in Galilee where Joseph, Mary, and the child settle after returning from Egypt, fulfilling the prophecy that he will be called a Nazarene.

l: Galilee, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Galilee, called 'Galilee of the Gentiles' in Isaiah's prophecy, is the region where Jesus withdraws after John's arrest, fulfilling the light-dawning prophecy. He calls his first disciples by its sea, teaches and heals throughout it, and later meets the eleven on a mountain there, commissioning them.

l: Israel, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: is_described_as lost sheep [destination of the disciples' mission] The house of Israel is described as lost sheep, and the disciples are sent only to it, not to Gentiles or Samaritan cities. Jesus says the disciples will not have gone through the cities of Israel before the Son of Man has come.

l: star, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Jesus's star, seen in the east by wise men as a sign of the King of the Jews' birth. It leads them, stops over the young child's location, and brings them great joy; Herod learns when it appeared.

l: massacre of male children, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: targets male children of Bethlehem [two years old and under, in Bethlehem and surrounding countryside] Herod, angered at being mocked by the wise men, sends out and kills all the male children two years old and under in Bethlehem and the surrounding countryside, based on the exact time he learned from the wise men. This is said to fulfill Jeremiah's words about a voice heard in Ramah, with Rachel weeping for her children who are no more.

l: John the Baptizer, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: John the Baptizer is a prophet and forerunner of Jesus, foretold by Isaiah as the voice crying in the wilderness. He preaches repentance in the wilderness of Judea, wears camel's hair with a leather belt, eats locusts and wild honey, and baptizes in water, rebuking the Pharisees and Sadducees. He announces a mightier one coming and baptizes Jesus after first objecting. Later, imprisoned by Herod for telling him it was unlawful to have Herodias, his brother's wife, he hears of Christ's works and sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one. Jesus affirms him as more than a prophet, the messenger preparing the way, greater than anyone born of women, and the Elijah who is to come, though some dismissed him as having a demon for neither eating nor drinking. The multitude regards him as a prophet. He is beheaded in prison; his disciples bury him and tell Jesus. His baptism later traps the leaders, who did not believe him though tax collectors and prostitutes did.

l: Jordan, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The Jordan is where people from Jerusalem, Judea, and the surrounding region are baptized by John while confessing their sins. It is also where Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized, and where the heavens open over him.

l: Pharisees and Sadducees, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: is_described_as offspring of vipers [said by John] Many Pharisees and Sadducees come to John for his baptism. John calls them offspring of vipers, asks who warned them to flee the coming wrath, and tells them to produce fruit worthy of repentance and not to rely on having Abraham as father.

l: people from Jerusalem, Judea, and the Jordan region, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: are_baptized_by John the Baptizer [in the Jordan, confessing their sins] People from Jerusalem, all of Judea, and the region around the Jordan go out to John. They are baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.

l: Kingdom of Heaven, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The Kingdom of Heaven is the central subject of Jesus's preaching in these records, proclaimed as Good News in the synagogues of Galilee with a call to repent because it is at hand. It is also described as the place of the Father and called God's Kingdom. It belongs to the poor in spirit, to those persecuted for righteousness' sake, and to little children and ones like them. Entry demands righteousness exceeding that of the scribes and Pharisees and requires turning and humbling oneself like a child. A rich man enters with difficulty, and some make themselves eunuchs for its sake. Within it, those who keep and teach even the least commandments are called great, those who break them least, and the least member is greater than John. Since John's days it suffers violence, and the violent take it by force. Its places beside Jesus are for those whom his Father has prepared. Most of the records are parables. It is likened to a field with good seed and darnel, a mustard seed that becomes a tree, yeast in meal, hidden treasure, a valuable pearl, and a dragnet. These images show small beginnings, worth giving up everything for, and a final separation of righteous and wicked. It is also likened to a king settling accounts, a master hiring laborers (the last first, the first last), a king's wedding feast, and ten virgins awaiting the bridegroom, some ready and admitted, others not. Several parables end with many called but few chosen. Overall it moves from announcement, to its conditions and members, to its contested status, to parables of growth, value, reversal, and judgment.

l: baptism, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: is_for repentance [John's baptism in water] John baptizes people in the Jordan in water for repentance, with confession of sins. He says the one coming after him will baptize in the Holy Spirit. Jesus is baptized by John, and the heavens open afterward.

l: repentance, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: John's message is "Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!" He tells the Pharisees and Sadducees to produce fruit worthy of repentance, warning that trees not producing good fruit are cut down and cast into the fire. His water baptism is described as being for repentance.

l: God, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: God, called the heavenly Father, is the supreme, perfect and uniquely good Lord of heaven and earth, whose throne is heaven and who owns the Kingdom. The records present him as Jesus's Father and the one Father of the disciples. Nothing is impossible for him, and he is the God of the living, not the dead, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the God of Israel. The account begins with his character: he is perfect and impartial, sending sun and rain on evil and good, just and unjust. He is seen by the pure in heart, and peacemakers are called his children. It then turns to his care and attentiveness. He sees secret giving, prayer and fasting and rewards them openly. He knows needs before people ask, feeds the birds, clothes the grass of the field, and gives good things to those who ask, far more than human parents do. He forgives those who forgive and withholds forgiveness from those who do not. He is not to be served alongside Mammon, and entering the Kingdom of Heaven requires doing his will. The middle of the records stresses his relationship with Jesus and his disciples. His Spirit speaks in disciples under trial. He knows each sparrow and numbers their hairs. Jesus will confess before him those who confess Jesus. Jesus thanks him for hiding things from the wise and revealing them to infants, as was well-pleasing to him, and says the Father has delivered all things to the Son, whom alone he knows and who reveals him. Later, God is the source of commandments, such as honoring parents, which tradition voids. He will uproot every plant he did not plant, and the crowds glorify him after the healings. His angels see his face, and he does not will that any little one perish. He answers agreed prayer. He made people male and female and joins husband and wife. No one is good but God alone, and the rich enter his Kingdom with difficulty. Finally, Jesus says to give God what is God's, that the Sadducees do not know his power, and that in the resurrection people are like God's angels.

l: voice from the heavens, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: declares_jesus_to_be beloved Son [well pleased] After Jesus's baptism, a voice out of the heavens says, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased."

l: Satan, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Satan, the devil and tempter, tempts Jesus three times with bread, the temple pinnacle, and worldly kingdoms; Jesus rebukes him as Satan, and he departs.

l: temptation of Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: After fasting forty days and nights and becoming hungry, Jesus is tempted three times: to command stones to become bread, to throw himself down from the temple pinnacle, and to worship the devil for all the kingdoms of the world. He answers each with 'It is written' and a quotation from Scripture, and the devil then leaves while angels come and serve him.

l: high mountain (of the transfiguration), The Gospel According to Matthew
s: is_a high mountain [site of Jesus's transfiguration] The high mountain is where Jesus takes Peter, James, and John by themselves. There he is transfigured, Moses and Elijah appear, and the voice speaks from the cloud. The group comes down from it afterward.

l: Capernaum, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Capernaum is a seaside place in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali. Jesus leaves Nazareth and settles there, fulfilling Isaiah's words. Later he addresses it as exalted to heaven yet destined to go down to Hades, warning its judgment will be more severe than Sodom's despite its mighty works.

l: Peter, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Peter, also called Simon and Simon Bar Jonah, is a fisherman and the brother of Andrew. Jesus sees him casting a net in the sea of Galilee, promises to make him a fisher of men, and Simon immediately leaves his nets and follows. He becomes a disciple, is listed first among the apostles, and addresses Jesus as Lord. Jesus gives him the name Peter, the rock. His story is one of bold faith mixed with failure. He walks on water but sinks in fear; he declares Jesus the Christ, the Son of the living God, and is promised the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, yet soon rebukes Jesus and is called a stumbling block. He accompanies Jesus up the high mountain with James and John, is sent to catch a fish with a stater for the temple tax, asks how often to forgive (seventy times seven), and notes that the disciples have left everything. At the end he vows never to stumble, sleeps in Gethsemane, follows Jesus at a distance, denies him three times as foretold, and weeps bitterly when the rooster crows.

l: Andrew, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Andrew, a fisherman and brother of Simon Peter, is seen casting a net by Jesus, called to fish for men, and immediately leaves his nets to follow.

l: James, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: James, son of Zebedee and brother of John, is mending nets in a boat with them when Jesus calls him; he immediately leaves his father and follows Jesus.

l: John, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: John, son of Zebedee and brother of James, is mending nets with his father when Jesus calls him; he immediately leaves both and follows.

l: call of the first disciples, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Walking by the sea of Galilee, Jesus calls two pairs of fishermen brothers: Simon Peter and Andrew, then James and John, the sons of Zebedee. Jesus tells the first pair to come after him and he will make them fishers for men, and both pairs immediately leave their nets, and in the second case their boat and father, to follow him.

l: multitudes (crowds around Jesus), The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Great multitudes gather to Jesus by the sea, standing on the beach while he teaches from a boat. He speaks to them only in parables, and then sends them away.

l: Jesus' healing ministry, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Jesus' healing ministry spans Galilee, where he heals every disease and sickness, including demon-possession, epilepsy, and paralysis. His fame spreads into Syria, and the sick are brought to him, drawing great multitudes from many regions to follow him.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The disciples are the followers of Jesus, a group that grows from learners into commissioned messengers. Early on they follow him, practice no fasting while the bridegroom is with them, and are taught on the mountain, where they are called the salt of the earth and the light of the world and told to let their good works shine so the Father is glorified. They are defended when they pluck grain on the Sabbath, and Jesus calls them his mother and brothers. They are given the mysteries of the Kingdom, receive explanations of the parables, and say they understand. They distribute the loaves Jesus blesses, then worship him in the boat as the Son of God. Their understanding is repeatedly imperfect: they misread the warning about yeast, are told to tell no one he is the Christ, are taught to deny themselves and take up the cross, and fail to cast out a demon because of lack of faith. Peter, James, and John fall in fear at the voice from the cloud. They are sorry at the prediction of his death, react to teachings on divorce, rebuke those bringing children, and are astonished about the rich. Jesus promises they will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. On the Mount of Olives they ask privately about the end of the age and are warned of hatred and told to watch. At the end the eleven go to the Galilee mountain, bow to Jesus though some doubt, and receive the commission to make disciples of all nations, baptize, and teach all he commanded.

l: Beatitudes, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Verses 3-10 give a series of blessings: the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the gentle, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and the persecuted. Each is paired with a promise, such as comfort, inheriting the earth, mercy, seeing God, and being called children of God. Verses 11-12 extend the blessing to those reproached and persecuted for Jesus's sake, who are told to rejoice because their reward in heaven is great.

l: law, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: endures_until all things are accomplished [not even smallest letter passes away] Jesus states he did not come to destroy the law or the prophets but to fulfill them. Not the smallest letter or pen stroke will pass from the law until all things are accomplished. Breaking even the least commandments and teaching others to do so makes one least in the Kingdom, and Jesus then reinterprets several commands from the law.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The Pharisees are a group portrayed throughout these records chiefly as opponents of Jesus. They are known for fasting often, and they come to Jesus repeatedly, sometimes with scribes from Jerusalem, Sadducees, or Herodians. In Chapter 9 they question his eating with tax collectors and sinners and claim he casts out demons by the prince of the demons. In Chapter 12 they accuse his disciples over the Sabbath, ask about healing on it, conspire to destroy him, attribute his exorcisms to Beelzebul, and ask for a sign; Jesus calls them offspring of vipers. In Chapter 15 they charge his disciples with breaking the elders' tradition; Jesus calls them hypocrites, says they make void God's commandment through tradition, honor him with lips while their hearts are far away, teach men's rules as doctrine, and are blind guides. In Chapter 16 they test him with a request for a sign, and he warns of their teaching. In Chapter 19 they test him on divorce. In Chapter 22 they seek to entrap him over taxes, send a lawyer, and finally cannot answer his question about the Christ.

l: righteousness, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled, and those persecuted for righteousness' sake are blessed. Jesus says the righteousness of his hearers must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees for them to enter the Kingdom of Heaven.

l: murder and anger, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: incurs judgment [murder and anger without cause] Jesus cites the command 'You shall not murder' and the danger of judgment for murder. He extends it to anger at a brother without cause, saying 'Raca!' or 'You fool!', each bringing danger of the judgment, the council, or the fire of Gehenna. He instructs that one should leave a gift at the altar and first be reconciled with a brother, and should settle quickly with an adversary to avoid prison.

l: adultery and lust, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: includes lustful gazing [counts as adultery in the heart] Jesus cites 'You shall not commit adultery' and says that anyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery in his heart. He says it is more profitable to lose an eye or a hand that causes stumbling than for the whole body to be cast into Gehenna.

l: divorce, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: is_permitted_for sexual immorality [only exception stated by Jesus] Jesus recalls the saying that whoever puts away his wife should give her a writing of divorce. He teaches that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, makes her an adulteress, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

l: oaths, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Oaths are a teaching of Jesus: swearing is forbidden entirely. After recalling not to make false vows but keep vows to the Lord, he bans swearing by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or one's head, requiring plain Yes and No.

l: retaliation, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: is_rejected_by Jesus [replaces eye for an eye] Jesus quotes 'An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth' and replaces it with a teaching not to resist the one who is evil. He instructs turning the other cheek, giving one's cloak as well as one's coat, going two miles when compelled to go one, and giving to those who ask or wish to borrow.

l: love of enemies, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: is_commanded_by Jesus [includes blessing and praying for persecutors] Jesus contrasts the saying 'love your neighbor and hate your enemy' with a command to love enemies, bless those who curse, do good to those who hate, and pray for persecutors. This makes his hearers children of the Father, who gives sun and rain to all. He notes that loving only those who love you, or greeting only friends, is what even tax collectors do, and concludes that his hearers should be perfect as the Father is perfect.

l: evil and adulterous generation, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: A group characterized as seeking signs and acting hypocritically: they sound trumpets when giving, pray in synagogues and street corners, and disfigure faces when fasting, all to be seen and gain glory from men, and so have already received their reward.

l: charitable giving, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: should_be_done in secret [not before men to be seen] Charitable giving, called merciful deeds, is not to be done before men to be seen by them, or no reward comes from the Father. It should be done so secretly that the left hand does not know what the right does, and the Father who sees in secret will reward it openly.

l: prayer, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Prayer is a topic in Chapter 6: it should be done in secret, in an inner room with the door shut, not to be seen, and avoid vain repetitions, since the Father knows needs beforehand.

l: Lord's Prayer, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The Lord's Prayer is a model prayer given as a pattern, addressed to Our Father in heaven. It asks for his name to be holy, his Kingdom to come, daily bread, forgiveness as we forgive, and deliverance from temptation and the evil one, ending with praise.

l: fasting, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: should_be_done in secret [anoint head and wash face] Fasting is not to be done with a sad, disfigured face like the hypocrites, who want to be seen fasting. Instead one should anoint the head and wash the face so that only the Father, who sees in secret, knows, and he will reward it.

l: forgiveness, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Forgiveness is a reciprocal condition: in the prayer about debts, people forgive debtors as they ask forgiveness; the Father forgives those who forgive others and withholds forgiveness from those who do not.

l: treasure, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Treasure is what one values; earthly treasure is vulnerable to moth, rust and thieves, so listeners are told to store it in heaven, safe from loss, because the heart follows the treasure's location.

l: anxiety, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Anxiety about life's needs (food, drink, clothing) and tomorrow is forbidden. Chapter 6 argues it is futile, unable to add a moment to life, since the Father feeds birds and clothes lilies; Gentiles seek these, and each day has enough evil.

l: God's Kingdom, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: God's Kingdom is a topic of Jesus' teaching. In Chapter 6 it is prayed for, belongs to the Father with power and glory, and is to be sought first with his righteousness, with needs then given. In Chapter 21 tax collectors and prostitutes enter before the leaders, and it is taken from them and given to a fruit-producing nation.

l: judging others, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: results_in being judged [same measure applied back] Jesus commands not to judge, so as not to be judged, and says people will be judged and measured by the same measure they use. He illustrates this with the speck in a brother's eye and the beam in one's own, calling the one who ignores his own beam a hypocrite who must first remove it to see clearly.

l: narrow gate and broad way, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: A pair of contrasting paths in Chapter 7: Jesus urges entering the narrow gate leading to life, which few find, rather than the broad way to destruction, which many enter.

l: false prophets, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: False prophets disguise themselves as sheep while inwardly being ravening wolves; Jesus warns in Chapter 7 to beware them and know them by fruits.

l: trees and fruit, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: A teaching image of trees and fruit in Chapter 7: Jesus says grapes don't come from thorns nor figs from thistles. Good trees bear good fruit, corrupt trees evil fruit, and trees without good fruit are cut down and burned, so people are known by their fruits.

l: those who say 'Lord, Lord', The Gospel According to Matthew
s: A group who call Jesus 'Lord, Lord' and cite prophesying, exorcisms, and mighty works, yet are excluded from the Kingdom of Heaven; Jesus rejects them as never known, workers of iniquity, since only doing the Father's will suffices.

l: wise man, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: A wise man, likened by Jesus to anyone who hears and does his words, builds his house on rock, which stands firm against rain, floods, and wind.

l: foolish man, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: A parable figure who hears Jesus's words but doesn't act on them, builds his house on sand, and it collapses greatly in the storm.

l: house on the rock, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: withstands storm [founded on the rock] The house on the rock was struck by rain, floods, and winds but did not fall, because it was founded on the rock. It represents the life of one who hears and does Jesus's words.

l: house on the sand, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: falls_in storm [its fall was great] The house on the sand was beaten by rain, floods, and winds and fell, and its fall was great. It represents the life of one who hears Jesus's words and does not do them.

l: Jesus's teaching, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Jesus's teaching, marked by authority unlike the scribes, covers not judging, asking, the golden rule, the narrow way, false prophets, and doing his words, and astonishes the multitudes.

l: leper, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: has_condition leprosy [cleansed by Jesus] A leper comes to Jesus, worships him, and says that if Jesus wants to, he can make him clean. Jesus touches him and says "Be made clean," and his leprosy is immediately cleansed; Jesus tells him to tell nobody, show himself to the priest, and offer the gift Moses commanded.

l: centurion, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: A centurion in Capernaum, a man under authority who commands soldiers, asks Jesus to heal his paralyzed, tormented servant, saying he is unworthy to host Jesus and a word suffices. Jesus marvels at his great faith, greater than Israel's, and the servant is healed that hour.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The disciples are the followers of Jesus, whom he calls people of little faith. In Chapter 8 they follow him into a boat, panic in a storm, wake him, and marvel when he calms the sea. In Chapter 15 the Pharisees accuse them of not washing hands before eating bread. Peter asks for an explanation, they urge sending the Canaanite woman away, doubt there is enough bread, then distribute loaves and fish.

l: Moses, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Moses, a lawgiver who stated the levirate marriage law, appears talking with transfigured Jesus on the mountain; Peter proposes a tent, then only Jesus remains.

l: storm at sea, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: A violent storm comes up on the sea so that the boat is covered with waves while Jesus sleeps. Jesus rebukes the wind and the sea, and there is a great calm.

l: possessed men of the Gergesenes, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Two exceedingly fierce demon-possessed men of the Gergesenes, living in tombs so that nobody could pass that way, meet Jesus, who commands the demons out of them.

l: demons, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The demons in the two men cry out to Jesus as Son of God and ask whether he has come to torment them before the time. They beg to be sent into the herd of pigs, and when Jesus says "Go!" they come out and enter the pigs. Demons are cast out by Jesus, whom the Pharisees say does so by Beelzebul, prince of the demons. Jesus says he does it by the Spirit of God, showing that God's Kingdom has come. He also describes an unclean spirit that leaves a man, returns, and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself.

l: herd of pigs, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: has_size many A large herd of pigs is feeding far from the possessed men. When the demons enter them, the whole herd rushes down the cliff into the sea and dies in the water.

l: city, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: has_attitude rejects Jesus [begged him to depart from their borders] Those who fed the pigs flee into the city and report everything, including what happened to the possessed men. All the city then comes out to meet Jesus and, on seeing him, begs him to depart from their borders.

l: healing of the sick, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Jesus heals the leper, the centurion's servant, and Peter's wife's mother, and in the evening heals all who are sick among those brought to him. This is said to fulfill Isaiah's words, "He took our infirmities and bore our diseases."

l: paralytic (man brought to Jesus), The Gospel According to Matthew
s: has_condition paralyzed [lying on a bed] A paralyzed man lying on a bed is brought to Jesus, who, seeing the faith of those bringing him, tells him his sins are forgiven. Jesus then tells him to get up, take his mat, and go home, and he rises and departs to his house.

l: ruler, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: has_child ruler's daughter A ruler comes and worships Jesus, telling him that his daughter has just died and asking him to come lay his hand on her so that she will live. Jesus gets up and follows him to his house.

l: ruler's daughter, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The ruler's daughter has just died when her father asks Jesus to come. Jesus says she is sleeping, not dead, and after the crowd is sent out he takes her by the hand and she arises, and the report spreads through the land.

l: woman with discharge of blood, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: has_condition discharge of blood [for twelve years] A woman who has had a discharge of blood for twelve years comes up behind Jesus and touches the fringe of his garment, saying within herself that this will make her well. Jesus turns, calls her daughter, tells her to cheer up because her faith has made her well, and she is made well from that hour.

l: two blind men, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: has_condition blind [healed by Jesus] Two blind men follow Jesus calling out for mercy as the son of David, and in the house they tell him yes when he asks if they believe he is able to do this. He touches their eyes and says it will be done according to their faith, and their eyes are opened. Despite his strict command to tell no one, they spread his fame throughout the land.

l: forgiveness of sins, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Jesus declares the paralytic's sins forgiven, which leads some scribes to say he blasphemes. Jesus says he heals the man so that they may know the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, and the multitudes glorify God for giving such authority to men.

l: twelve disciples, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The twelve disciples are the apostles Jesus names and sends out, giving them authority over unclean spirits and disease. They preach that the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand, travelling without money or provisions, like sheep among wolves. They are warned of hatred, trials and betrayal, and promised the Father's Spirit will speak through them. Later they protest the anointing, prepare the Passover, and each asks if he is the betrayer. They sleep in Gethsemane, and all flee at Jesus' arrest despite vowing otherwise.

l: Judas Iscariot, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve disciples, betrays Jesus to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver. At the meal he asks if it is him and is told 'You said it.' He leads an armed crowd and identifies Jesus with a kiss. Seeing Jesus condemned, he feels remorse, returns the silver, is refused, throws it in the sanctuary, and hangs himself.

l: Son of Man, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The Son of Man is a figure who will come at an unknown day and hour, so people must watch; he arrives in glory with all the holy angels and sits on his glorious throne.

l: persecution of the disciples, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: involves scourging in synagogues [also trials before governors and kings] Jesus predicts the disciples will be sent as sheep among wolves, scourged in synagogues, brought before governors and kings, and hated by all for his name's sake. Family members will deliver one another to death. They are told to flee from city to city, not to fear those who kill the body, and that those who endure to the end will be saved.

l: reward for receiving disciples, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: is_given_for receiving a prophet, righteous man, or disciple [a prophet's, righteous man's reward; cup of cold water] Jesus teaches that whoever receives the disciples receives him and the one who sent him. Those who receive a prophet or righteous man as such will receive that person's reward, and whoever gives even a cup of cold water to a disciple will in no way lose his reward. Worthy households that welcome the disciples receive their peace, while those who reject them face a judgment worse than Sodom and Gomorrah.

l: this generation, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: This generation is likened by Jesus to children in marketplaces whose companions refuse to dance or mourn. It rejects John the Baptizer as demon-possessed for fasting, then rejects the Son of Man as a glutton and drunkard, friend of sinners; judgment is to come upon it.

l: Chorazin, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Chorazin is a place where Jesus performed mighty works yet it did not repent. He pronounces woe on it, saying Tyre and Sidon would have repented, so they will face a more tolerable judgment than Chorazin.

l: Bethsaida, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Bethsaida is a place where mighty works were done but people did not repent; Jesus pronounces woe on it, saying Tyre and Sidon would have repented and will face a more tolerable judgment.

l: mighty works (Jesus' mighty works), The Gospel According to Matthew
s: includes healing the blind, lame, lepers, deaf, raising the dead [works John's disciples heard and saw] Jesus' works, including the blind seeing, the lame walking, lepers cleansed, the deaf hearing, the dead raised, and good news preached to the poor, are what he cites in answer to John. Most of them were done in the cities that did not repent, which Jesus denounces, saying that Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom would have responded to them.

l: those who labor and are heavily burdened, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Jesus invites all who labor and are heavily burdened to come to him, promising to give them rest. He tells them to take his yoke and learn from him, and says they will find rest for their souls.

l: rest, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Jesus promises rest to all who labor and are heavily burdened if they come to him. He says that by taking his yoke and learning from him, they will find rest for their souls.

l: yoke (Jesus' yoke), The Gospel According to Matthew
s: Jesus' yoke is an easy, light burden he offers the weary; taking it and learning from his gentle, humble heart brings rest for souls.

l: Sabbath, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: The Sabbath is the occasion of two disputes: the disciples' plucking of grain and the healing of the withered hand. Jesus argues that the priests profane it and are guiltless, that a man is worth more than a sheep, and that it is lawful to do good on it. He declares that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.

l: man with a withered hand, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: has_condition withered hand [restored whole by Jesus] The man with a withered hand is in the synagogue when the Pharisees ask whether healing on the Sabbath is lawful. Jesus tells him to stretch out his hand, and it is restored whole like the other.

l: nations, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: All the nations will be gathered before the Son of Man on his throne. He will separate them one from another as a shepherd separates sheep from goats.

l: possessed man, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: has_condition blind and mute [possessed by a demon; healed by Jesus] A man possessed by a demon, blind and mute, is brought to Jesus. Jesus heals him so that he both speaks and sees, and the multitudes are amazed and ask whether Jesus is the son of David.

l: Beelzebul, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: is_a prince of the demons Beelzebul is named by the Pharisees as the prince of the demons, by whom they claim Jesus casts out demons. Jesus replies that Satan casting out Satan would be a divided kingdom that cannot stand.

l: sign from heaven (requested by the Pharisees and Sadducees), The Gospel According to Matthew
s: is_withheld_except Jonah [only the sign of the prophet Jonah] The Pharisees and Sadducees asked Jesus to show them a sign from heaven to test him. Jesus refused, saying no sign would be given to that evil and adulterous generation except the sign of the prophet Jonah, and then left them.

l: farmer (parable of the sower), The Gospel According to Matthew
s: A farmer goes out to sow seed, which falls on the roadside, rocky ground, among thorns, and on good soil. In Jesus's account, the farmer's sowing illustrates how people hear the word of the Kingdom.

l: parable of the sower, The Gospel According to Matthew
s: explains_seeds_by_roadside hearer who doesn't understand the word [evil one snatches the word] Jesus tells of seed that is devoured by birds, scorched for lack of root, choked by thorns, or yields thirty, sixty or one hundred times on good soil. He explains that these are people who hear the word and fail to understand, fall away under persecution, are choked by cares and riches, or understand and bear fruit.

l: seeds (sown by the farmer), The Gospel According to Matthew
